notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 2 Chronicles 23, drawn from the sources I was able to access. I did not find significant denominational disagreements on this chapter (most traditions read this historical narrative similarly), nor was I able to reach Catholic/Orthodox or modern scholarship sites on this occasion.

---

**GENERAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE CHAPTER**

The chapter parallels 2 Kings 11:4–20, but the Chronicler emphasises the role of priests and Levites, whereas Kings emphasises the military (the Carites, royal guards, and couriers). Precept Austin notes that “Kings records the fall of a tyrant. Chronicles records the revival of a nation” — the Chronicler adds the gathering of Levites from all Judah, detailed Levitical guard assignments, the renewal of temple worship, and an explicit appeal to God’s promise to David (v. 3). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-23-commentary)

Dr. Constable observes that the Chronicler had little interest in Athaliah herself since she was not of the Davidic line (she was Ahab’s daughter); his concern was with events that brought the next Davidic king, Joash, to the throne. He also notes that the temple “was a visual symbol of the continuity of the Davidic dynasty.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-23.html)

---

**VERSES 1–3: Jehoiada gathers allies and makes a covenant**

**v. 1 — “In the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself and made a covenant with the commanders of hundreds…”**

Jehoiada “strengthened himself” — the Hebrew verb *chazaq* means to be strong, to show oneself courageous. Ellicott notes this is a favourite expression of the Chronicler (*hithchazzaq*), replacing Kings’ simpler “Jehoiada sent.” The Pulpit Commentary says he “nerved himself with courage, and that courage which results from conviction of duty and of ripe time to achieve it.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

The five named commanders correspond to the five detachments mentioned in Kings (three “third parts” plus “two parts” of another body), probably summing to a force of nominally five hundred. Of none of these five is anything known beyond this honourable mention. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

F. B. Meyer (quoted at Precept Austin and Enduring Word) says: “The easiest thing for Jehoiada would have been to shut himself up in the temple, and leave things to take their course. The noblest thing was to come forth, and boldly confront the rampant evil of his time.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-23-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

Matthew Henry commends Jehoiada as a man of great prudence (reserving the prince six years until the nation was weary of Athaliah), great interest (the captains, Levites, and chiefs joined him), great faith (his eye was on God’s promise to David), and great religion (he insisted on temple sanctity even during a coup). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-23.html)

**v. 2 — “They went throughout Judah and gathered the Levites…and the heads of the families of Israel…”**

This verse is entirely the Chronicler’s addition; Kings makes no mention of the Levites here. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Chronicler “is sure to signalize” the Levites. Ellicott agrees: the Chronicler supplemented the Kings account with material from other authorities, perhaps Levitical traditions. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 3 — “The whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God…”**

This is the second, wider covenant — the first was between Jehoiada and the five captains (v. 1). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the existence of Joash was probably news to those gathered; the parallel in Kings says Jehoiada “showed them the king’s son,” so “double significance lies in the word ‘showed.’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

“Behold, the king’s son shall reign, as the LORD promised concerning the descendants of David.” Jehoiada grounds the coup not merely in political legitimacy but in God’s covenant promise to David through Nathan (2 Samuel 7). David Guzik notes that one reason Athaliah had reigned for six years was that nobody knew there was an alternative — and that many people “live under the reign of Satan because they don’t really know there is a legitimate king ready to take reign in their lives.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

---

**VERSES 4–7: Jehoiada’s plan for the coup on the Sabbath**

**v. 4 — “A third of you priests and Levites who come on duty on the Sabbath shall keep watch at the doors…”**

The Chronicler specifies “priests and Levites,” while Kings speaks of the royal guard. Ellicott suggests the Chronicler may have found it impossible that any but members of the sacred orders would be summoned into the Temple by the high priest, though he may also have had a source that emphasised the priestly role. The Pulpit Commentary observes that “the distinct and repeated mention of the Levites” marks the Chronicler’s account. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 5 — “A third shall be at the royal palace, and a third at the Foundation Gate…”**

The “king’s house” here probably does not mean the royal palace but the part of the temple complex where Joash had been hidden for six years. The Pulpit Commentary argues this: “the last clause in each of vv. 5, 6, 7 in the parallel go strongly to confirm the position that ‘the king’s house’ so far does not intend the royal palace.” The “Gate of the Foundation” (Hebrew *yesod*) is thought to be the same as the “Gate Sur” in Kings — probably a corruption of the Hebrew word. It stood at the corner of the area strengthened by additional works, where the ravine separated Moriah from the hill to the south. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 6 — “No one is to enter the house of the LORD except the priests and those Levites who serve…”**

This verse has no parallel in Kings. Ellicott says it “looks like a protest against 2 Kings 11:4, where it is said that Jehoiada brought the centurions of the royal guard into the house of the Lord.” The Chronicler, from a strict legalist perspective, insists only consecrated personnel may enter the sanctuary proper. Matthew Henry notes that Jehoiada “gave special order that none of the people should come into the house of the Lord, but the priests and Levites only… Never let sacred things be profaned, no, not for the support of civil rights.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-23.html)

**v. 7 — “The Levites must surround the king with weapons in hand, and anyone who enters the temple must be put to death.”**

Kings says “ye shall compass the king” (addressing the centurions). The Chronicler says “the Levites shall compass the king.” The Pulpit Commentary argues that Kings implicitly needs the word “Levites” there — “its significance perhaps accidentally overlooked.” Ellicott suggests the truth may be that Jehoiada “brought about a combination of the royal guard with the Levitical warders of the Temple; and that the united body acted under the command of the five centurions of the guard.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm)

---

**VERSES 8–11: Joash is crowned**

**v. 8 — “So the Levites and all Judah did everything that Jehoiada the priest had ordered… for Jehoiada the priest had not released any of the divisions.”**

“Dismissed not the courses” means the companies of priests and Levites whose weekly duties had ended were detained as auxiliaries. Under ordinary circumstances they would have been formally dismissed. By retaining both the incoming and outgoing divisions, Jehoiada doubled his available force without arousing suspicion. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

David Guzik notes: “Jehoiada chose the Sabbath for the day of the coup, because that was the day when the guards changed their shifts and they could assemble two groups of guards at the temple at the same time without attracting attention.” Trapp adds: “It was a weighty work he went about, and therefore he took the wisest course, the fittest time; on the Sabbath, when the congregation met; and in the temple, whither Athaliah and her courtiers seldom came.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

**v. 9 — “Jehoiada the priest gave to the commanders of hundreds the spears and the large and small shields of King David that were in the house of God.”**

These weapons had been stored in the temple as trophies or dedications from David’s campaigns (perhaps the shields of gold David took from Hadadezer’s servants, 2 Samuel 8:7, 11). Guzik notes it was fitting for soldiers restoring David’s line to use weapons that had belonged to David himself. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

**v. 10 — “He stationed all the troops…surrounding the king by the altar and the temple, from the south side to the north side…”**

The guard was placed on the south and north sides of the temple. “Along by the altar” refers to the altar of burnt offering in front of the porch, near which the young king would stand “at his pillar” (v. 13). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 11 — “Then Jehoiada and his sons brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, presented him with the Testimony, and proclaimed him king.”**

Guzik traces the pattern of Joash’s coronation: (1) he was *brought out* — revealed to the people; (2) the *crown* was placed on him — public recognition; (3) he was given *the Testimony* — the word of God (a copy of the Law, as Deuteronomy 17:18 requires the king to have); (4) he was *made king* — received by the people; (5) he was *anointed* — divine empowerment; (6) they shouted *“Long live the king!”* — he received praise. Guzik applies this pattern to receiving Jesus as King. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

The “Testimony” (*ha-‘eduth*): The Pulpit Commentary says “it is quite unnecessary…to suppose that the testimony, as well as the crown, was put on the head of Joash. It may be taken for granted that the testimony was put into his hands.” The Cambridge Bible notes it was “probably some document testifying to the promises” — a kind of charter. Ellicott adds the Vulgate reading: “they put upon him the diadem and the testimony, and gave into his hand the law to be held.” The custom of presenting a Bible to the monarch survives in British coronations. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

---

**VERSES 12–15: Athaliah’s death**

**v. 12 — “When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and cheering the king, she went out to them in the house of the LORD.”**

Athaliah heard the commotion from the royal palace. That she came alone (or at least unguarded) into the temple courts suggests she did not suspect a coup. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-23.html)

**v. 13 — “She looked out and saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance.”**

The “pillar” was a platform or stand where the king was elevated to be seen by the assembly — a customary place for the monarch in the temple court (cf. 2 Kings 23:3; 2 Chronicles 34:31). The Chronicler alone mentions “the singers with musical instruments…leading the praises” — a characteristic addition reflecting his interest in temple music. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed “Treason! Treason!” (*qesher* — “conspiracy”). The Pulpit Commentary notes the charge was factually correct: this was treason against her government, but “a well-founded and godly treason against a tyrannical, wicked ruler.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/)

**v. 14 — “Bring her out between the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her… She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.”**

Jehoiada’s concern for the sanctity of the temple — even in executing a usurper who had murdered the royal family and promoted Baal worship — reflects “a great concern for the sanctity and reputation of the temple.” The unusual prepositional phrase likely means: “Have her forth from inside the house of the Lord to within your ranks.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 15 — “They seized Athaliah as she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate to the palace grounds, and there they put her to death.”**

The Horse Gate was the entrance for the king’s horses/mules. The Pulpit Commentary notes that “in the place where horses entered, they killed her there” — an ignominious end for the daughter of Jezebel. G. Campbell Morgan is quoted: “Her own treason against the true and abiding King of the nation was defeated. Thus, sooner or later…the moment arrives when those who plot and plan against Heaven and righteousness, find themselves looking at the evidences of the triumph of God and of goodness over all their wickedness.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm)

---

**VERSES 16–17: Covenant renewal and destruction of Baal worship**

**v. 16 — “Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people.”**

The wording differs from Kings, which reads “between the LORD and the king and the people.” The Chronicler writes “between himself” (Jehoiada), viewing the high priest as representing the LORD in the transaction, which “avoids the apparent irreverence of making the Deity a direct co-partner with men in a compact.” Kings also adds “and between the king and the people,” a clause about limitations of royal prerogative usually agreed upon at the start of a reign (cf. 1 Samuel 10:25). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm)

Selman is quoted: “The climax is not Joash’s coronation but a covenant renewing the nation’s relationship with God.” Payne adds: “Along with Jehoiada’s political revolution came a corresponding religious revival — that king, priest, and citizenry would together ‘be the LORD’s people.’” Benson’s Commentary explains: “Jehoiada, as God’s priest, was his representative in this transaction, or a sort of mediator, as Moses was. God covenanted by him to take them for his people; and the king and people covenanted with him to be his.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-chronicles-23.html)

**v. 17 — “All the people went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols…and killed Mattan the priest of Baal.”**

The temple of Baal in Jerusalem had apparently been erected alongside the very temple of the LORD — probably under Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:6) or Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 22:3), since Athaliah was granddaughter of a Tyrian king (Ethbaal). The destruction included not only the building but the sacred objects and the priest. Payne notes that killing Mattan “carried out the requirement of God’s Word directed against those who should lead others into false religion (Deuteronomy 13:5-10).” Grant’s Commentary observes: “This negative work was necessary, just as was the execution of Athaliah, before the positive establishment of the true worship of God.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-23.html)

---

**VERSES 18–19: Restoration of proper temple worship**

**v. 18 — “Jehoiada put the oversight of the house of the LORD into the hands of the Levitical priests…to offer burnt offerings…as is written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and song, as ordained by David.”**

This verse is a thorough expansion of the brief Kings notice: “And the priest appointed officers over the house of the LORD.” The Chronicler emphasises that Jehoiada restored worship according to two authorities: (1) the Law of Moses for sacrifices, and (2) the order of David for music and singing. Ellicott notes: “The meaning of all this is that the high priest now restored the regular services of the Temple, as arranged by David, which had been neglected or at least irregularly conducted during the six years of Athaliah’s usurpation.” Benson’s Commentary adds that under Athaliah those temple offices “had probably been disposed of to persons of other tribes, partly to gratify their wicked friends, and partly to bring God’s house and worship into disgrace.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-chronicles-23.html)

**v. 19 — “He stationed gatekeepers at the gates…so that nothing unclean could enter for any reason.”**

The gatekeepers ensured that no ceremonially unclean person entered the temple (cf. Leviticus 5:7; Numbers 5:19). Trapp comments: “Oh that we also had store of such porters, to keep out the unclean from holy ordinances!” Grant’s Commentary applies this to the Church: “We always need discernment as to what should be allowed in and what must be refused entry.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-23.html)

---

**VERSES 20–21: The king enthroned and the city at peace**

**v. 20 — “They brought the king down from the house of the LORD…through the Upper Gate…and seated King Joash on the royal throne.”**

“The Upper Gate” (called “the gate of the guard” in Kings) was probably the grand entrance to the palace, perhaps the same as the temple gate of 2 Chronicles 27:3. The procession moved from the temple to the palace — the rightful king going from God’s house to the king’s house. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/23.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/23.htm)

**v. 21 — “All the people of the land rejoiced. And the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword.”**

“The city was quiet” — this was a relatively bloodless revolution apart from Athaliah and Mattan; no civil war erupted. Selman notes: “That the city was quiet was a sign of God’s blessing, which often followed special acts of faith and obedience (cf. 1 Chronicles 4:40; 22:9; 2 Chronicles 13:12; 14:4-5; 20:30).” Constable adds: “All the people of the land rejoiced, a characteristic response found in Chronicles whenever the Lord’s will was being followed.” Grant’s Commentary observes: “How instructive is the fact that when a wicked ruler dies the people rejoice!” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-23/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-23.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-23.html)

---

**DENOMINATIONAL DIFFERENCES AND OTHER VIEWS**

I did not find substantive denominational disagreements on this chapter from the approved sources. The narrative is historical, and Protestant traditions (Baptist, Reformed, Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran) tend to read it the same way. The one area where a nuance appears is v. 16 — the covenant. Kings reads “between the LORD and the king and the people”; Chronicles reads “between himself and the king and the people.” Reformed covenantal theologians might emphasise this as a theocratic covenant renewal, while some Baptist commentators (like Garner-Howes) simply note it historically. Benson’s (Methodist-leaning) Commentary explains Jehoiada acted as mediator representing God, a pattern seen with Moses. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-chronicles-23.html)

I was unable to access Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) within the available search and fetch limits for this chapter.

---

**SUMMARY OF KEY THEMES**

1. **God preserves His promise.** The Davidic line survived through six years of Athaliah’s reign because of God’s covenant faithfulness (v. 3). The hidden Joash illustrates that God’s purposes often work unseen before public vindication.

2. **Courageous leadership.** Jehoiada “strengthened himself” — a deliberate act of courage rooted in conviction, not passivity. He did not remain safely in temple service while evil reigned.

3. **Holiness and reverence.** Even during a coup, Jehoiada insisted that only consecrated persons enter the sanctuary and that Athaliah not be executed within the temple precincts. Sacred things must not be profaned for civil purposes.

4. **Reformation follows revolution.** Removing the usurper (Athaliah) and false worship (Baal’s temple) was only the negative work; the positive work was restoring worship according to Scripture (Law of Moses) and godly tradition (order of David).

5. **Joy and peace follow righteousness.** The people’s rejoicing and the city’s quiet were twin marks of God’s blessing when His will was done.
